pos: n. (a swift hound; in Proverbs 30, one of four things comely in going)
etymology: From Old Norse grey, a bitch or dog, and hound; the grey has nothing to do with colour. The Hebrew is literally girt in the loins, a creature built for running, and the Authorized Version names it greyhound once, in Agur's list of things that go well.
biblical_def: Agur numbers three things which go well, yea, four are comely in going: a lion which is strongest among beasts and turneth not away for any, a greyhound, an he goat also, and a king against whom there is no rising up. The list is about bearing. Each of the four moves through the world without flinching, and Agur has an eye for the particular dignity of each gait — the lion's refusal to yield ground, the hound's stretched speed, the he goat at the head of the flock, the king whose progress nobody contests. Proverbs is full of this kind of looking. The same chapter admires four things little upon the earth but exceeding wise: the ants, the conies, the locusts, the spider. Agur does not moralise the greyhound with a lesson; he sets it in a list and lets the reader feel the comeliness of a creature doing exactly what it was made to do. That is itself a doctrine. God made kinds, and every kind has a proper motion and a proper excellence, and the wise man notices. The chapter's next verse supplies the only warning the list needs: if thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, lay thine hand upon thy mouth.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a tall, fleet dog kept for the chase, remarkable for swiftness and keenness of sight; in Scripture, one of the four comely goers of Proverbs 30.
webster_full: GREYHOUND, n. A tall fleet dog, kept for the chase.
COMELY, a. Handsome; graceful; decent; suitable; becoming.
GAIT, n. A going; a walk; a march; a way; manner of walking or stepping.
HOUND, n. A generic name of the dog; but in English it is confined to a particular breed used in the chase.
STATELY, a. Lofty; dignified; majestic; magnificent in mien or manner.
scriptures: A greyhound; an he goat also; and a king, against whom there is no rising up.
There be three things which go well, yea, four are comely in going:
There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
corruption_summary: Creation is treated as raw material valued only by its usefulness to man, so that the sheer fittedness and beauty of a creature is left out of the account; Proverbs 30 stops and admires the way a hound runs.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a utilitarian flattening of the created order that measures a beast entirely by yield, and there is an opposite sentimentality that levels man and beast into one moral class. Proverbs 30 does neither. Agur is a man watching animals with pleasure and drawing wisdom from the watching, and the pleasure is not a detour from the wisdom. He sees that a hound is comely in going, that ants are exceeding wise, that a conies' refuge in the rock is well chosen. The doctrine underneath is Genesis 1: God made every creature after his kind and saw that it was good, and the goodness is in the creature itself before it is ever in the use.

The fourth item in the list is where the chapter turns toward man, and it cuts against every reader. A king against whom there is no rising up walks with the same unhesitating dignity as the lion. Agur sets human majesty among the animals, not above them, and then immediately addresses the man who has lifted up himself and thought evil, and tells him to lay his hand upon his mouth. Proverbs 16 says the same without the picture: pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
roots_summary: Hebrew zarziyr mothnayim (H2223, H4975), girt in the loins, rendered greyhound; yatab (H3190), to go well; 'ariy (H738), a lion.
roots_lines: Hebrew zarziyr (H2223) — girt, tight-loined; with mothnayim, the greyhound of Proverbs 30:31.
Hebrew mothnayim (H4975) — the loins; the seat of a creature's strength and speed.
Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to be good, to go well; three things which go well.
Hebrew tsa'ad (H6806) — a pace, a step, a going; comely in going.
Hebrew layish (H3918) — a strong lion; first of the four.
usage: “A greyhound; an he goat also” — the single occurrence, in Agur's list.
“three things which go well” — the frame of the saying.
The greyhound as an emblem of a creature perfectly fitted to its motion.

pos: n. (the female lion; in Ezekiel 19, a figure of the royal mother of Judah)
etymology: From lion with the feminine ending. The Authorized Version uses it once, at the head of Ezekiel's lamentation for the princes of Israel, where the question What is thy mother? is answered with a single word.
biblical_def: Take up a lamentation for the princes of Israel, and say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions. The figure is a royal house, and Ezekiel is careful about how it was raised. She lay down among lions, which is to say she took her place in the company of the surrounding predatory kings, and she nourished her whelps in that company. The whelps grew into what they were fed. One became a young lion, learned to catch the prey, and devoured men; the nations took him in their pit and brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt. She waited, and took another of her whelps, and made him a young lion, and he did the same, and they put him in ward in chains and brought him to the king of Babylon, that his voice should no more be heard upon the mountains of Israel. The lamentation is over a mother's formation of her sons. She taught them to hunt as the nations hunt, and the nations caught them both. Ezekiel calls the poem a lamentation, and it shall be for a lamentation, because what is being buried is a dynasty raised on the wrong instincts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the female of the lion kind; in Scripture, Ezekiel's figure for the royal mother whose whelps became devourers and were taken.
webster_full: LIONESS, n. The female of the lion kind.
WHELP, n. The young of the dog kind and of lions and other beasts of prey.
LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
NOURISH, v.t. To feed and cause to grow; to supply with nutriment; to educate.
PREY, n. Spoil; booty; that which is seized by violence to be devoured.
scriptures: Eze 19:2
And say, What is thy mother? A lioness: she lay down among lions, she nourished her whelps among young lions.
Eze 19:3
And she brought up one of her whelps: it became a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men.
Eze 19:9
And they put him in ward in chains, and brought him to the king of Babylon: they brought him into holds, that his voice should no more be heard upon the mountains of Israel.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
corruption_summary: Parental formation is reduced to affection and provision, as though what a child is taught to admire were morally neutral; Ezekiel 19 lays a dynasty's ruin at the feet of a mother who nourished her whelps among lions.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel does not accuse the lioness of neglect. She nourished her whelps; she brought one up; she waited and took another and made him a young lion. The care is real and the outcome is catastrophic, because she formed them in the company she had chosen to lie down among. Scripture's doctrine of nurture is never merely provision. Fathers are commanded to bring children up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, which is a formation of loves and not only a supply of needs, and Ezekiel shows the alternative formation doing its work in one generation.

The second thing the chapter refuses is the flattery of strength. Both whelps learned to catch the prey and both devoured men, and by the world's reckoning they were successful young lions until the moment the nations dropped a net on them. Predatory competence is not safety. Peter takes the same animal and puts it where the dictionary puts it: your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. A house that raises lions has misjudged which lion is actually loose in the world.
roots_summary: Hebrew labiy' (H3833), a lioness or great lion; gowr (H1482), a whelp; qiynah (H7015), a dirge or lamentation.
roots_lines: Hebrew labiy' (H3833) — a lioness, a great lion; the mother of Ezekiel 19:2.
Hebrew gowr (H1482) — a whelp, a cub; her sons in the figure.
Hebrew kephiyr (H3715) — a young lion, one old enough to hunt; what each whelp became.
Hebrew qiynah (H7015) — a dirge, a lamentation; the form of the whole chapter.
Hebrew taraph (H2963) — to tear, to catch prey; it learned to catch the prey.

“she nourished her whelps among young lions” — the formation that ruined them.
“as a roaring lion, walketh about” — the lion the church is actually warned of.

pos: n. (a large bloodsucking leech; the emblem of insatiable appetite)
etymology: From horse, denoting the large kind, and leach, the old spelling of leech, a bloodsucking worm. The Authorized Version uses it once, at the head of Agur's numerical saying on the things that are never satisfied.
biblical_def: The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough. The four follow: the grave, the barren womb, the earth that is not filled with water, and the fire that saith not, It is enough. Agur's picture is a creature whose whole existence is a mouth, and whose two daughters have learned exactly one word and say it twice. The list that follows universalises the appetite. Death never has enough, barrenness never has enough, dry ground never has enough, fire never has enough, and the reason the four are gathered is that human desire is like them. Ecclesiastes states it without the figure: he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he that loveth abundance with increase. Habakkuk applies it to an empire, of a proud man who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations. The doctrine is not that desire is evil. It is that desire aimed at anything under the sun has no floor, and only God is large enough to be a bottom to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the large leech, so called because it fastens on horses; in Scripture, Agur's emblem of a craving that never says It is enough.
webster_full: HORSELEECH, n. A large leech which fastens on horses; also, a farrier.
LEECH, n. A blood-sucking worm; also, a physician, from the ancient use of leeches.
INSATIABLE, a. Incapable of being satisfied or appeased; very greedy.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good.
SATISFY, v.t. To gratify wants, wishes or desires to the full extent; to content.
scriptures: The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough:
The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, It is enough.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
Hab 2:5

Yea also, because he transgresseth by wine, he is a proud man, neither keepeth at home, who enlargeth his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all people:
corruption_summary: Acquisition is presented as a path to contentment provided the target is reached, when Scripture teaches that appetite pointed at created things has no resting point at all — the horseleach's daughters never stop crying.
corruption_paragraphs: The advertisement, the salary review, and the upgrade all rest on a single unstated premise: that there exists an amount which would be enough. Proverbs 30 denies it by analogy and Ecclesiastes denies it by observation. He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver, and the clause that follows is the sharper one — nor he that loveth abundance with increase. The problem is not the size of the holding but the direction of the love. A soul made for God will treat every created thing as if it ought to be God, and will therefore consume it and cry give again.

Habakkuk takes the same appetite up to national scale and shows where it ends, in a man who enlargeth his desire as hell and gathereth unto him all nations, and then in the woe that follows. The biblical cure is not a smaller appetite but a sufficient object. Paul learned contentment in whatsoever state he was, and the ground he gives is not resignation but a Person: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. The dictionary therefore treats covetousness as idolatry, which is where Colossians puts it, and not as a merely economic habit.

“four things say not, It is enough” — the frame of the saying.
“He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver” — the same doctrine without the figure.

pos: n. (the young hatched at once and gathered under the hen)
etymology: Old English brod, from the root of breed; the hatching, and then the hatched. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Luke, in the Lord's lament over Jerusalem, where he compares himself to a hen and the city to a brood that would not come.
biblical_def: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not. Matthew records the same words with her chickens under her wings. The figure is deliberately domestic and deliberately weak: not an eagle, not a lion, but a hen, whose only defence is to spread herself over the young and take on her own body whatever comes. Christ chooses the image of a protector who shields by being struck. The whole of the atonement is inside it. And the clause the Lord adds is the one the dictionary will not soften: and ye would not. Two wills are in the sentence, his willing to gather and theirs refusing to come, and the tears are real. He wept over the city in the next chapter of Luke and said, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace. The Old Testament figure lies behind it — he shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust — and so does the eagle of Deuteronomy 32 that stirreth up her nest and beareth them on her wings.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): offspring; progeny; the young hatched at once, as of a hen; in Scripture, the figure of Christ's gathering of Jerusalem.
webster_full: BROOD, n. Offspring; progeny; formerly used of human beings in elegant writers.
BROOD, n. The young birds hatched at once; a hatch; as a brood of chickens.
HEN, n. The female of any kind of fowl; but the word is applied to the domestic fowl by way of eminence.
GATHER, v.t. To bring together; to collect a number of separate things into one place or into one aggregate body.
WING, n. The limb of a fowl by which it flies; in Scripture, a figure of protection and covering.
scriptures: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
Psa 91:4
He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:
corruption_summary: The lament over Jerusalem is used to argue that God's saving will is always frustrated by the human will, or else the human refusal is explained away; the text holds both the sincere gathering and the real ye would not, and blames the refusal on the refusers.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a favourite proof text in the argument against particular redemption, and it will not carry the weight put on it. Christ addresses Jerusalem, the city and its leaders who killed the prophets, and says he would have gathered thy children — the ones those leaders kept from coming. The rebuke falls on men who stood between the hen and the brood. Reformed theology has never denied that God commands all men everywhere to repent, that the gospel offer is sincere, or that Christ wept genuine tears over a city that refused him. What it denies is that the refusal is ever the last word about anyone the Father has given to the Son, for all that the Father giveth me shall come to me.

The opposite error is to hear ye would not and quietly remove its force, as though human refusal were a formality. It is not. Jerusalem is guilty, and the guilt is the point of the lament. Scripture holds the two together without embarrassment and so does the dictionary: men are responsible, and salvation is of the Lord. The figure itself decides the tone. A hen spreading her wings is not a distant decree; it is a body offered, and the cross is where the striking fell.

pos: n. (a small deer with palmate antlers; a clean beast, and meat for Solomon's table)
etymology: From fallow, pale brownish-yellow, and deer. The Authorized Version spells it as one word once, among the daily provisions of Solomon's house, and as two words in the list of clean beasts in Deuteronomy 14.
biblical_def: Solomon's daily provision included ten fat oxen, and twenty oxen out of the pastures, and an hundred sheep, beside harts, and roebucks, and fallowdeer, and fatted fowl. The fallowdeer is a clean beast, listed in Deuteronomy 14 with the hart, the roebuck, the wild goat, the pygarg, the wild ox, and the chamois, and so lawful food; the point of its appearance in 1 Kings is scale. This is one day at one table. The chapter is describing a kingdom at the height of the promise, dwelling safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, with Solomon's wisdom exceeding the wisdom of all the children of the east. And the same book records what the table cost and what it became, for the provision of that house is part of the burden that broke the kingdom in two under his son. Ecclesiastes, written by the man who ate that venison, gives the verdict from the inside: whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, and then, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit. The fallowdeer is therefore a small entry on a long invoice, and the invoice is instructive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a species of deer smaller than the stag, of a pale yellowish-brown colour; in Scripture, a clean beast and part of Solomon's daily provision.
webster_full: FALLOW, a. Pale red or pale yellow; as a fallow deer.
DEER, n. A quadruped of the genus Cervus, of several species, as the stag or red deer, the fallow deer and the roebuck.
VENISON, n. The flesh of deer; game; the flesh of beasts of chase taken in hunting.
PROVISION, n. Victuals; food; provender; all manner of eatables for man and beast.
CLEAN, a. In the Jewish law, free from ceremonial defilement; lawful to be eaten.
scriptures: Ten fat oxen, and twenty oxen out of the pastures, and an hundred sheep, beside harts, and roebucks, and fallowdeer, and fatted fowl.
Deu 14:5
The hart, and the roebuck, and the fallow deer, and the wild goat, and the pygarg, and the wild ox, and the chamois.
And Solomon's provision for one day was thirty measures of fine flour, and threescore measures of meal,
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
corruption_summary: Material abundance is read as the settled evidence of divine approval, so that a full table ends the question; the same Scripture that records Solomon's provision records what the provision cost the nation and what the king concluded about it.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 4 is genuine blessing, and the dictionary will not sour it. Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon, and this is held out as the near approach of the peace God promised. Abundance is not a sin and the fallowdeer on the table is not a rebuke. The error is to treat the table as the proof rather than the gift, which the prosperity teaching does explicitly and which most of us do quietly. Deuteronomy had already warned the nation about what full barns do to the memory: when thou hast eaten and art full, then beware lest thou forget the LORD.

The rest of the history is the argument. The provision of one day grew into a levy the tribes could not bear, and Rehoboam's refusal to lighten it split the kingdom. The king who ate the venison wrote afterwards that he had withheld nothing his eyes desired and found it vanity, and that he that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver. Scripture gives us the table, the bill, and the verdict, and a doctrine of prosperity that keeps only the first is not reading the book.

pos: n. (in gier eagle, an unclean bird of the law, probably the Egyptian vulture)
etymology: From the old word gier or gyr, a vulture, related to the German Geier. The Authorized Version uses it only in the compound gier eagle, twice, in the two lists of unclean fowls.
biblical_def: And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle. So Leviticus, and Deuteronomy repeats it: and the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant. The gier eagle is a carrion bird, and it appears only in the two catalogues of fowls which Israel was to have in abomination and not eat. The lists are long and tedious to read, and the tedium is part of their instruction. God took the trouble to name the eagle, the ossifrage, the ospray, the vulture, the kite, the raven after his kind, the owl, the night hawk, the cuckow, the hawk, the little owl, the cormorant, the great owl, the swan, the pelican, the gier eagle, the stork, the heron, the lapwing, and the bat. Israel was to know the difference by sight, at a glance, in the field, all day long. That is what Leviticus means when it says, Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean. The dietary law was a daily drill in discrimination, training a people to see a line where the nations saw none, and the birds that fed on death were on the far side of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the gier eagle, a bird named among the unclean fowls of the Mosaic law, understood to be a species of vulture.
webster_full: GIER-EAGLE, n. A fowl of the eagle or vulture kind, reckoned unclean by the Mosaic law.
VULTURE, n. A genus of fowls, ranked in the order of Accipiters, which feed on carrion.
UNCLEAN, a. In the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; not lawful to be eaten or touched.
ABOMINATION, n. That which is abominable; an object of extreme disgust or hatred.
DIFFERENCE, n. The state of being unlike or distinct; distinction; disagreement.
scriptures: And the swan, and the pelican, and the gier eagle,
And the pelican, and the gier eagle, and the cormorant,
And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,

Ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and between unclean fowls and clean: and ye shall not make your souls abominable by beast, or by fowl, or by any manner of living thing that creepeth on the ground, which I have separated from you as unclean.
corruption_summary: The dietary lists are dismissed as arbitrary taboo, or spiritualised so completely that the habit they trained is lost; the law itself gives the reason, which is to teach a people to put difference where the nations put none.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings do the same damage from opposite directions. The first treats Leviticus 11 as primitive food superstition, arbitrary and therefore safely ignored. The second grants it meaning but evaporates it, so that clean and unclean become an abstraction with no residue in how anyone lives. Leviticus 20:25 blocks both: ye shall therefore put difference between clean beasts and unclean, and the sentence after it names the point — ye shall be holy unto me, for I the LORD am holy, and have severed you from other people. The drill was in discrimination, daily, by sight, until distinguishing was second nature.

The New Testament ends the food law and keeps the trained faculty. Christ declared all meats clean, and the sheet let down to Peter settled it for the Gentiles, so no Christian is bound by the gier eagle. But Hebrews describes the mature as those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil, which is the same drill moved inward. A generation taught that judging anything is the only sin has lost the faculty the bird lists existed to build, and it did not gain charity by losing it.

pos: adj. (bitten or wasted by hunger; famished)
etymology: From hunger and bitten, the past participle of bite — hunger pictured as a thing with teeth. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Bildad's speech against Job, describing the end of the wicked man.
biblical_def: His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction shall be ready at his side. Bildad is describing the fate of the wicked, and the phrase is vivid and cruel: not that the man is hungry, but that his strength itself is bitten, gnawed away from within, while ruin waits at his elbow. The next verse presses it further — it shall devour the strength of his skin, even the firstborn of death shall devour his strength. As a general description of what sin does to a man, Bildad is not wrong; Scripture says elsewhere that the young lions do lack, and suffer hunger, but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing. What Bildad is wrong about is the application. He is using true doctrine as a diagnosis of a specific righteous man in the ash heap in front of him, and God says at the end of the book that Bildad and his friends have not spoken of him the thing that is right, as Job hath. The word therefore serves the dictionary twice: as an unforgettable picture of the wasting that follows wickedness, and as a warning about the pastoral use of true sentences.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): pinched or wasted by hunger; starved; used once in Scripture of the wicked man's strength in Bildad's speech.
webster_full: HUNGERBITTEN, a. Pinched or weakened by hunger.
HUNGER, n. An uneasy sensation occasioned by the want of food; a craving of food.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient to sustain the people of a country.
DESTRUCTION, n. Demolition; a pulling down; ruin; the state of being destroyed.
AFFLICTION, n. The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief.
scriptures: His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction shall be ready at his side.
It shall devour the strength of his skin: even the firstborn of death shall devour his strength.
The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing.
Mat 5:6
Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled.
corruption_summary: Suffering is read backwards as proof of secret sin, the friends' method in the book of Job; Scripture keeps the general truth that wickedness wastes a man and denies that affliction is a reliable verdict on any particular sufferer.
corruption_paragraphs: Bildad's speech is orthodox and misapplied, which makes it more dangerous than heresy. Every clause of it could be defended from Proverbs. The wicked really are brought down, their light really is put out, their strength really is bitten by hunger in the end. The failure is in the inference: this man is suffering, therefore this man is wicked. God's own verdict closes the book against the three friends and for Job, and the Lord himself refused the same inference when asked who sinned, the blind man or his parents, answering that neither had, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.

The error is alive in two modern dresses. One is the prosperity teaching, which reads health and money as evidence of favour and therefore must read illness and poverty as evidence of the reverse. The other is a therapeutic version that treats every hardship as a symptom to be traced to a cause in the sufferer. The Reformed answer is providence: afflictions are real, purposeful, and fatherly toward the elect, and their meaning is not readable off their surface. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled — a hunger with a promise attached, which Bildad had no category for.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'eb (H7457), hungry or famished; 'own (H202), strength or vigour; 'eyd (H343), calamity or destruction.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'eb (H7457) — hungry, famished; with 'own, his strength shall be hungerbitten.
Hebrew 'own (H202) — vigour, wealth, generative strength; what hunger bites.
Hebrew 'eyd (H343) — calamity, destruction; ready at his side.
Hebrew bekowr maveth (H1060, H4194) — the firstborn of death; Bildad's name for the worst disease.
Hebrew chacer (H2637) — to lack, to want; they that seek the LORD shall not want.
usage: “His strength shall be hungerbitten” — the single occurrence, in Bildad's second speech.
“The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger” — the promise Bildad had no room for.
Hungerbitten as a picture of strength gnawed away from within.

pos: adj. (eaten and spoiled by moths; of hoarded garments)
etymology: From moth and eaten. In the Authorized Version it describes the wardrobes of the rich in James's indictment, where the clothing has been kept so long that the moth has had it.
biblical_def: Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten. James is writing to rich men who have hoarded in the last days, and the picture is of wealth destroying itself in storage. Grain rots, cloth is eaten, and the next verse turns the metal itself into a witness: your gold and silver is cankered, and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days. The charge that follows is concrete and not abstract — the hire of the labourers who reaped the fields, which is kept back by fraud, crieth, and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. Riches are not condemned as such; hoarded riches and withheld wages are. The Lord had said the same on the mount: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal. Isaiah puts the moth beside the only thing it cannot eat — the moth shall eat them up like a garment, but my righteousness shall be for ever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): eaten or gnawed by moths; in Scripture, the state of hoarded garments in James's indictment of the rich.
webster_full: MOTHEATEN, a. Eaten or gnawed by moths.
MOTH, n. An insect of many species, some of which eat and destroy woollen cloth.
CANKER, v.t. To corrode; to corrupt; to eat, as rust does metal.
HOARD, v.t. To collect and lay up a large quantity of anything in a repository.
TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve.
scriptures: Jas 5:2
Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten.
Jas 5:3
Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.
Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Isa 51:8
For the moth shall eat them up like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool: but my righteousness shall be for ever, and my salvation from generation to generation.
corruption_summary: Saving is defended in the abstract until the distinction between provision and hoarding disappears, and the specific sin James names — wages kept back from the men who reaped the fields — goes unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: James 5 is not an attack on property, and reading it that way has done real harm. Scripture commends the ant that provideth her meat in the summer, requires a man to provide for his own house, and treats inheritance as a good thing to leave. What James indicts is treasure heaped together while wages are held back, and he is precise about the mechanism: the hire of the labourers is kept back by fraud, and it cries, and the cry has reached the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. The moths and the rust are simply the evidence that the wealth was doing nothing except sitting, while the men who earned it went unpaid.

The corruption running the other way is the sanctified version of hoarding that calls itself stewardship, in which every year's surplus is retained on the grounds of prudence and the barn is never opened. Christ told a parable about that man and called him a fool the night his soul was required. The dictionary's line follows the Lord's own: lay up treasure in heaven, pay what is owed, provide for your house, and hold the rest loosely, because where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
roots_summary: Greek setobrotos (G4598), moth-eaten; sepo (G4595), to rot or corrupt; ios (G2447), rust or poison.
roots_lines: Greek setobrotos (G4598) — moth-eaten; the one occurrence, James 5:2.
Greek ses (G4597) — a moth; where moth and rust doth corrupt.
Greek sepo (G4595) — to putrefy, to rot; your riches are corrupted.
Greek ios (G2447) — rust, poison, venom; the rust shall be a witness against you.
Greek thesaurizo (G2343) — to lay up treasure, to hoard; ye have heaped treasure together.
usage: “your garments are motheaten” — the single occurrence, in James's indictment.
“where moth and rust doth corrupt” — the Lord's own use of the same insect.
“the moth shall eat them up like a garment” — Isaiah, against the fear of men.

pos: n. (the cry of a horse; in the prophets, a figure of lust and of invasion)
etymology: From neigh, an imitative word for the cry of a horse. Jeremiah uses it twice over, once of the sound of an invading cavalry and once, in the plural, of the adulteries of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land. Jeremiah is describing the invasion from the north, and he describes it by sound. Before an army is seen it is heard, and the sound that carries furthest across a plain at night is the noise of the horses. But Jeremiah has already used the same animal for something else: they were as fed horses in the morning; every one neighed after his neighbour's wife. And later the LORD says plainly, I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom. The prophet has bound two things together with one sound. The nation that neighed after its neighbours' wives will hear the neighing of the horses that come to take it away. Judgment in Jeremiah is very often the sin returned in kind and enlarged. And the verse that indicts the nation's heart is the one that stings most: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the cry or voice of a horse; in Scripture, both the sound of an invading army and a figure for unbridled lust.
webster_full: NEIGHING, n. The voice of a horse; a whinnying.
NEIGH, v.i. To utter the voice of a horse, called whinnying.
SNORTING, n. The act of forcing the air violently through the nose, as a horse.
LEWDNESS, n. The unlawful indulgence of lust; fornication or adultery.
INVASION, n. A hostile entrance into the possessions of another; particularly, the entrance of a hostile army.
scriptures: Jer 8:16

The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land, and all that is in it; the city, and those that dwell therein.
Jer 5:8
They were as fed horses in the morning: every one neighed after his neighbour's wife.

I have seen thine adulteries, and thy neighings, the lewdness of thy whoredom, and thine abominations on the hills in the fields. Woe unto thee, O Jerusalem! wilt thou not be made clean? when shall it once be?
Jer 8:6
I hearkened and heard, but they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle.
corruption_summary: Sexual sin is treated as a private matter with no public consequence, so that the link Jeremiah draws between a nation's adulteries and a nation's ruin is dismissed as prophetic exaggeration.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah refuses to keep the bedroom and the battlefield in separate chapters. Fed horses in the morning, every one neighing after his neighbour's wife, is his description of the men of Jerusalem in a season of prosperity, and the horses that come from Dan in chapter 8 are the answer to it. Scripture consistently treats sexual sin as a public act with covenantal weight, because marriage is a public institution and its breach unmakes households, and households are what a nation is made of. The modern separation of private morals from public consequence would have struck the prophet as a category error.

The sharper accusation is not the lust but the unrepentance around it. I hearkened and heard, but they spake not aright: no man repented him of his wickedness, saying, What have I done? That is the sentence that fixes the doom, and the figure Jeremiah chooses for it is the same animal again — every one turned to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle. A people can be warned, can hear, and can still run, and the running looks like momentum and is actually blindness. The dictionary names the remedy the prophet names: ask the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein.
roots_summary: Hebrew metsahalah (H4684), a neighing; tsahal (H6670), to neigh or cry shrill; na'aph (H5003), to commit adultery.
roots_lines: Hebrew metsahalah (H4684) — a neighing; the sound of the invading cavalry, Jeremiah 8:16.
Hebrew tsahal (H6670) — to neigh, to cry shrilly; every one neighed after his neighbour's wife.
Hebrew na'aph (H5003) — to commit adultery; I have seen thine adulteries.
Hebrew zimmah (H2154) — a plan, and so lewdness, wickedness; the lewdness of thy whoredom.
Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to be sorry, to repent; no man repented him of his wickedness.
usage: “the sound of the neighing of his strong ones” — the invasion heard before it is seen.
“every one neighed after his neighbour's wife” — the same sound, the other sin.
“as the horse rusheth into the battle” — the figure for unrepentant momentum.

pos: v. (to stoop low, to cringe, to bow servilely)
etymology: From Old French crochir, to bend or become crooked. In the Authorized Version it is never a posture of worship but of servility — the bending of a man before another man for bread, or the stooping of a predator before a victim.
biblical_def: The word falls in the sentence on the house of Eli, and it is the most humiliating clause in it. Every one that is left in thine house shall come and crouch to him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread, and shall say, Put me, I pray thee, into one of the priests' offices, that I may eat a piece of bread. The priestly line that had helped itself to the fleshhook full of meat will beg for the smallest office in order to eat at all. And the principle God states in the same speech is the axis of the whole chapter: them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed. The Psalmist uses the word for the other kind of stooping, of the wicked man who lieth in wait secretly, who croucheth, and humbleth himself, that the poor may fall by his strong ones — a feigned lowliness that is a hunting posture. Both uses are the opposite of the fear of God. One is the cringing that follows contempt for God, and the other is a counterfeit humility used as a weapon, and Proverbs names the root of both: the fear of man bringeth a snare.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to bend down; to stoop low; to lie close to the ground; hence, to fawn, to bend servilely; to cringe.
webster_full: CROUCH, v.i. To bend down; to stoop low; to lie close to the ground.
CROUCH, v.i. To bend servilely; to stoop meanly; to fawn; to cringe.
CRINGE, v.i. To bow; to shrink; to make a servile obeisance.
SERVILE, a. Slavish; mean; fawning; such as proceeds from dependence.
HUMILITY, n. Freedom from pride and arrogance; a deep sense of one's own unworthiness.
scriptures: And it shall come to pass, that every one that is left in thine house shall come and crouch to him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread, and shall say, Put me, I pray thee, into one of the priests' offices, that I may eat a piece of bread.

Wherefore the LORD God of Israel saith, I said indeed that thy house, and the house of thy father, should walk before me for ever: but now the LORD saith, Be it far from me; for them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
He croucheth, and humbleth himself, that the poor may fall by his strong ones.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
corruption_summary: Humility is confused with cringing, so that a fawning deference to whoever holds bread is mistaken for a Christian grace; Scripture uses the crouching posture for servility and for predation, never for godly lowliness.
corruption_paragraphs: Biblical humility stands upright before men and bows before God. The crouching of 1 Samuel 2:36 is the collapse of a house that had it the other way round, and the crouching of Psalm 10:10 is a hunter's trick. Neither is the meekness Christ blesses. The counterfeit is easy to mistake because it produces agreeable people, but it is generated by the fear of man rather than the fear of God, and Proverbs says exactly what that fear is: a snare. A man who cannot say a hard thing to whoever controls his bread has already been captured, and the ministry is the place where the capture does most harm.

The chapter also supplies the positive rule, and it is unconditional in both directions: them that honour me I will honour, and they that despise me shall be lightly esteemed. Eli's house lost its honour because it took God's portion; the boy Samuel grew on before the LORD in the same building. Honour is not distributed by position or lineage but by the estimate a man makes of God, and it is finally God who adjusts the scales. That is the cure for cringing, and the only one.
roots_summary: Hebrew chachah (H7812 in form shachah, to bow down), and dakah (H1794), to crouch or be crushed; kabad (H3513), to honour or make heavy.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachah (H7812) — to bow down, to prostrate oneself; the posture of 1 Samuel 2:36.
Hebrew dakah (H1794) — to crouch, to be crushed or broken; the wicked man of Psalm 10:10.
Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy, to honour; them that honour me I will honour.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to be light, to be lightly esteemed; the opposite verdict.
Hebrew agowrah (H95) — a small coin, a piece of silver; what the crouching was for.
usage: “crouch to him for a piece of silver” — the sentence on the house of Eli.
“He croucheth, and humbleth himself” — feigned lowliness as a hunting posture.
“The fear of man bringeth a snare” — the root of both kinds of crouching.
